prose.article: ἐμπίπτω literally means to fall into something—a pit, a hole, or someone's hands—and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 7 times, all rendered "fall," both literally (a sheep falling into a pit in Matthew 12:11) and figuratively (falling into judgment or temptation in 1 Timothy). prose.def: The braiding or elaborate plaiting of hair as a form of adornment.

present charges or a legal case
reveal oneself / appear (middle-passive, relational or cultic)
prose.article: In the New Testament, ἐμφανίζω most often carries a legal or official sense — bringing charges, presenting a case, or filing a formal report to the authorities, which is why the Majority Standard Bible renders it with "case" or "presented their case" in most of its 10 occurrences. The word also has a broader range meaning "to make visible" or "to show oneself," as the older lexicons note (e.g. revealing oneself or appearing). The papyri confirm this courtroom flavor beautifully: a 221 BC petition uses the very same word for lodging an official complaint with the local magistrates, showing it was standard bureaucratic Koine.
prose.caution: With only 10 occurrences and 3 of them absorbed into phrasing without an English word of their own, the measured data reflects a narrow legal slice of a word whose wider "reveal/appear" sense rests mainly on the lexicons.

issues: SYNTACTIC ROLES anomaly: Macula data reports vocative (10×) for every occurrence, which is clearly a data artifact and cannot be taken at face value for a verb — this undermines confidence in the syntactic evidence

SENSE LABELS are too narrow: only the legal-report cluster is labeled (senses 1 and 2 together cover 4 of 10 occurrences), but 3 occurrences are absorbed and at least 3 rare renderings ('reveal','show') represent a distinct manifest/appear sense attested in JOH 14:21-22, MAT 27:53, HEB 9:24, HEB 11:14 — none of these are labeled as a sense
The definition's second clause ('reveal or show oneself') is mentioned but not given a sense label, leaving ~30–40% of occurrences without a matching labeled sense

The article claims the MSB renders the word with 'case' or 'presented their case' in 'most of its 10 occurrences' but the measured data shows only 4 of 10 occurrences are independently confirmed in those renderings — this overstates the legal dominance

KJV and Abbott-Smith both attest a clear passive/middle sense (appear before, show oneself) that is morphologically distinct and theologically significant (HEB 9:24 Christ appearing before God) but the definition does not distinguish active vs. middle/passive voice

receipts.how: Demonstrates the core legal-report sense: the Jewish leaders formally request (ἐμφανίζω) that the tribune bring Paul before them, confirming the quasi-technical official-report usage the definition centers on.

Demonstrates the reveal/manifest sense the definition mentions but does not label: Jesus promises to reveal (ἐμφανίσω) himself to the one who loves him — a personal, relational disclosure unrelated to legal reporting.

Shows the middle/passive 'appear before' sense the definition omits morphologically: Christ appears (ἐμφανισθῆναι) in God's presence on our behalf, a cultic-theological use distinct from both the legal and relational senses.

audit.author_note: Acts uses ἐμφανίζω exclusively in legal-administrative contexts (official reports and charges before Roman officials), while John and Hebrews use it for personal or cultic manifestation/appearance, so a definition framed primarily around the legal sense will mislead readers of John and Hebrews.

prose.def: Serving as a predicate adjective meaning full of fear or alarmed, describing a sudden state of fright or dread in response to a startling or awesome event.
prose.article: This word describes a person seized by fear or alarm, built from the parts "in" and "fear." Across its 6 New Testament occurrences the measured renderings split evenly between "frightened" and "terrified," though in 4 of those cases the fear is woven into the surrounding phrasing rather than a single English word. Abbott-Smith notes a wider range in older usage, listing "terrible" alongside "in fear," and a striking magical papyrus from the 2nd–3rd century even describes the moon itself becoming "full of fear" as the earth shakes.
prose.caution: The two measured senses each rest on a single occurrence and most uses are absorbed into phrasing, so the boundary between "frightened" and "terrified" is fuzzy rather than firm.

issues: The definition describes only an adjectival/participial state but ἔμφοβος functions as a predicate adjective in 5 of 6 occurrences; the definition should reflect this predicative role rather than implying a participial modifier
KJV attests 'tremble' as a distinct gloss not captured by either sense label or the definition, suggesting a physical-response nuance the current wording misses
BSB independently agrees with 'terrified' 0% of the time, undermining the confidence placed in that sense label; the two-label split rests on single occurrences each and overstates certainty
Abbott-Smith's sense 1 ('terrible') — an objective rather than subjective sense — is acknowledged in the article but silently dropped from the definition without explanation
The definition omits any signal that in 4 of 6 occurrences the word is absorbed into surrounding phrasing and carries no standalone English equivalent, which is the dominant pattern

receipts.how: Felix becomes ἔμφοβος while listening to Paul reason about judgment, functioning as a predicate adjective meaning 'frightened/alarmed,' the clearest match for the definition's core sense.

The women at the tomb are described as ἐμφόβων, absorbed into the narrative phrasing rather than rendered as a single English word, illustrating the dominant pattern the definition fails to foreground.

Survivors of the earthquake 'became ἔμφοβοι,' where BSB agrees 0% with 'terrified,' showing the second sense label lacks independent corroboration and its boundary with 'frightened' is unjustifiably sharp.

audit.author_note: Luke (Gospel + Acts) accounts for 5 of 6 occurrences and consistently uses ἔμφοβος as a predicate adjective describing sudden, visceral alarm in encounter scenes; Revelation's single use describes a communal response to catastrophe, suggesting a slightly broader, less personal register that the definition does not distinguish.

prose.def: To breathe upon or into someone or something, as when Jesus breathed on his disciples in John 20:22.
prose.article: This verb means to blow or breathe air at or onto a person or object. It appears just once in the New Testament, in John 20:22, where Jesus breathes on his disciples. The same word turns up in the Greek Old Testament six times, notably in Genesis 2:7 where God breathes life into the first human, and an everyday medical recipe in the papyri even uses it for blowing powdered hellebore into the nostrils to stop sneezing.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence, the measured sense rests on a single verse.

prose.def: Describing something inborn or implanted within a person; in its only NT use (Jas 1:21), applied to the received word, with 'inborn/natural' the sense best supported by documentary evidence.
senseLabels: inborn, natural (or possibly implanted from without)
prose.article: ἔμφυτος describes something rooted inside a person, built from the parts meaning "in" and "to grow." Its single New Testament appearance, in James 1:21, speaks of the implanted word, and the Majority Standard Bible renders it "moral" there. There's a genuine debate about its exact force: Abbott-Smith lists both "innate" and "rooted, implanted," and the papyri (such as one referring to "your natural kindness") favor the sense "inborn, natural" — which is why scholars like Hort argued for that meaning over "implanted from without."
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament and the evidence is thin, with sources genuinely divided over whether it means "inborn" or "implanted from outside."

prose.def: A preposition governing the dative meaning primarily 'in' (place, time, or state) but also 'on,' 'among,' 'with,' or 'by' (instrumentally), often absorbed into surrounding phrasing.
prose.article: ἐν is the workhorse preposition of the New Testament, appearing 2,786 times across all 27 books, and it overwhelmingly means "in" — 1,659 of its translated occurrences (98%). It marks position in space, time, or condition, but stretches to "with," "on," "by," and "among" depending on context. Notably, in 1,098 of those occurrences it carries no English word of its own, getting absorbed into the surrounding phrasing. In the Septuagint it is even more frequent (11,557 times) and stands in for the Hebrew prefix בְּ, including its pairing with words like "day" (524×) and "Jerusalem" (504×).
prose.caution: Moulton-Milligan calls it the "maid-of-all-work" among prepositions whose extended uses cannot be exhaustively catalogued, so its precise force in any given verse often depends on context.

audit.author_note: Paul uses ἐν with notable theological density — especially in phrases like 'in Christ' (ἐν Χριστῷ) — to express union and sphere of salvation, a nuance less prominent in Luke's spatially concrete or historically descriptive uses.

prose.def: To take someone into one's arms; to enfold or embrace, used in the New Testament only of Jesus receiving children.
senseLabels: to take children in one's arms (MAR 10:16)
prose.article: This verb means to fold or take someone into your arms — a physical embrace. In the New Testament it appears just twice, both in Mark, where Jesus takes children into his arms (Mark 9:36 and 10:16). The Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew חִבֻּק, and Moulton-Milligan notes it shows up in everyday Koine inscriptions, including one referring to embracing children.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin — only two New Testament occurrences, both in Mark, so the word's full range is hard to gauge.

receipts.how: Jesus takes a child and places him in the midst, then takes him in his arms — the verb's physical sense of enfold/receive into the arms is demonstrated clearly here.

prose.def: Belonging to or living in the sea; used of marine creatures.
prose.article: ἐνάλιος describes things that live in the sea, and in the New Testament it appears as the plural noun phrase "sea creatures." It shows up just once, in James 3:7, where it is part of a list of animal types humans have tamed. The word is built from ἐν ("in") and ἅλς ("the sea"), so it literally means "in the sea."
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament and not at all in the critical text, so its range cannot be measured beyond that single use.

prose.def: A preposition (with genitive) meaning 'before' or 'in the sight of,' indicating one party's position in the presence or view of another; also used adverbially.
prose.article: ἔναντι is a preposition (taking the genitive) meaning "before" or "in the presence of" — picturing one party standing face-to-face with another. It is rare in the New Testament but extremely common in the Septuagint, appearing 227 times, where it most often renders the Hebrew word for "face" (פָּנִים, 53×), which fits its sense of being in someone's presence. Moulton-Milligan note its appearance in everyday papyri and inscriptions — including a 170 BC translation of a Roman senatorial decree — proving the word was ordinary Koine and not confined to biblical Greek.
prose.caution: The word appears only once with its own force in the Byzantine NT, and editions disagree on its readings (some print the related ἐναντίον), so its NT distribution is uncertain.

issues: The definition omits the adverbial use of ἔναντι; Abbott-Smith classifies it as an adverb as well as a preposition, and the corpus shows it is sometimes absorbed into phrasing without yielding its own English word
The existing caution is well-placed but the definition itself does not acknowledge textual uncertainty or the overlap with ἐναντίον, which editors sometimes substitute (e.g., ACT 7:10 in WH)

With only 1–2 NT occurrences the definition leans heavily on LXX usage without noting this; the LXX also shows ἔναντι translating עֵדָה and נוּף, not only פָּנִים, so the 'face-to-face' gloss is an oversimplification of its full semantic range
The phrase 'face-to-face' implies mutual presence/confrontation but the word more precisely marks the spatial or relational vantage point of one party before another, not necessarily reciprocal

receipts.how: Zechariah serving 'before God' (ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ) shows the core sense of being in the presence/sight of a superior, supporting the genitive-preposition usage the definition describes
'Your heart is not right before God' (ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ) confirms the 'in the presence/sight of' meaning in the NT's clearest occurrence, matching Moulton-Milligan's citation
Textual disagreement here—WH prints ἐναντίον rather than ἔναντι—demonstrates the textual uncertainty the definition should acknowledge but currently buries only in the caution note

audit.author_note: Both NT occurrences appear in Lukan writings (Luke and Acts), so no cross-author variation can be measured; the definition cannot be tested against Pauline or Johannine usage.

prose.def: A preposition (with genitive) meaning 'before' or 'in the presence/sight of' someone, used of both human and divine witnesses.
prose.article: ἐναντίον works as a preposition meaning "before" or "in the presence of" someone, often carrying the sense of being in their sight or view. The measured New Testament renderings cluster tightly around this one idea, with the translation differences ("his," "before," "before His") simply reflecting the surrounding words. The Septuagint shows just how common this was, appearing 387 times and most often standing in for the Hebrew פָּנִים ("face," 159×), which fits the literal picture of being "in front of someone's face."
prose.caution: It is the neuter form of the adjective ἐναντίος ("opposite, hostile"), so context decides whether "before" or "contrary" is meant; the New Testament uses it only as the preposition.

prose.def: Set against something — either physically opposite or facing it (a contrary wind, a centurion across from Jesus), or figuratively hostile and adversarial to others.
prose.article: ἐναντίος describes one thing set against another, whether literally (a wind blowing against a boat) or figuratively (people who are hostile or opposed). It appears 8 times in the Byzantine New Testament, with the Majority Standard Bible rendering it "against" twice and "out" (as in "opposite," e.g. a centurion standing across from Jesus) twice. The Septuagint uses it about 60 times, most often translating the Hebrew נֶ֫גֶד ("in front of, opposite") 23 times; everyday papyri show it in oath formulas where "the reverse" or "the opposite" is meant, like "if I swear falsely, may the opposite happen."
prose.caution: Only 8 New Testament occurrences and split renderings mean the line between "facing/opposite" and "hostile/opposed" depends heavily on context.

prose.def: To begin or make a start on something, with possible but uncertain faint ritual overtone inherited from classical Greek usage.

In the Septuagint it appears 8 times across 5 books, where Abbott-Smith notes it chiefly renders a Hebrew word meaning to begin or profane. The most interesting wrinkle is that in classical Greek the word carried a ritual sense (beginning a sacrifice), and Moulton-Milligan suggests this may faintly linger in the two NT uses, though everyday Koine papyri show the plain sense begin had fully taken over.

prose.def: Lacking necessary resources; needy or poor, used of someone who lacks life's basic necessities such as food or money.

One papyrus poignantly records a family "being in want of 25 drachmas for the funeral of Philip," forced to sell his cuirass — capturing the word's ordinary sense of falling short of life's necessities.
prose.caution: The word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range there is narrow, though the Septuagint and papyri broaden the picture.

prose.def: A visible sign or proof that something is true, a concrete piece of evidence pointing to a conclusion.
prose.article: ἔνδειγμα refers to a tangible piece of evidence — a plain token or proof that demonstrates something is the case. It appears only once in the New Testament, at 2 Thessalonians 1:5, where the Majority Standard Bible renders it within the idea of something being "clear." Abbott-Smith notes a fine distinction: ἔνδειγμα (with its passive form) points to the *thing proved*, whereas the related ἔνδειξις refers to the *act of proving* itself.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its measured range rests on a single passage and confidence is low.

prose.def: The indeclinable number eleven, used in the NT exclusively for the group of apostles remaining after Judas, sometimes with an adverbial nuance ('meanwhile').
prose.article: ἕνδεκα simply means the number eleven, formed from the words for "one" and "ten," and it never changes its form. The everyday, non-biblical reach of the word shows up in the papyri: it appears on an ostracon receipt from A.D. 79 recording a poll-tax payment, written simply as the numeral.

prose.def: The ordinal number eleventh, marking something as eleven in a sequence or order.
prose.article: This is simply the ordinal number "eleventh," built from the word for "eleven" (ἕνδεκα). All three New Testament uses point to the same meaning: the eleventh hour in Jesus' parable of the laborers (Matthew 20:6, 9) and the eleventh foundation stone in Revelation 21:20. The everyday papyri show it doing the same plain work — dating documents to "the eleventh of the month" or recording "the eleventh hour of the day" — and in the Septuagint it translates the Hebrew expression for eleven (עַשְׁתֵּי) twelve times.
prose.caution: The three measured "senses" reflect surrounding words in the translation, not real differences in meaning; the word always simply means "eleventh."

receipts.how: Jesus asks why workers are standing idle at the eleventh hour, confirming the word means the ordinal position eleven in a sequence of hours.
Workers hired at the eleventh hour receive their pay, again using the word as a straightforward ordinal modifier, consistent with the definition.

prose.def: To prepare someone for burial, whether by anointing with perfume in anticipation or by wrapping a corpse with spices and linen according to burial custom.

prose.article: This verb covers the whole process of readying a corpse for burial — anointing, wrapping in cloth, and laying it to rest according to local custom. prose.def: An authoritative order or commandment — most often one of God's commandments, but also any binding directive from a human or institutional authority.
prose.article: ἐντολή is an authoritative directive — an order, injunction, or commandment. Of its 71 Byzantine occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "commandment" 53 times (82%) and "command" or "commanded" in nearly all the rest, so the meaning is remarkably stable. While the New Testament usually applies it to God's commandments, the broader range covers any authoritative instruction: everyday Koine papyri use it for a royal ordinance of a Ptolemaic king, and in the Septuagint it most often translates Hebrew מִצְוָה ("commandment," 128 times). The word is built on the verb ἐντέλλομαι ("to command").

receipts.how: Demonstrates the dominant sense: Jesus refers to 'one of the least of these commandments,' confirming ἐντολή as an authoritative divine precept, supporting the core definition.
The chief priests and Pharisees issue an ἐντολή ordering that Jesus be reported — a human, non-divine authority, showing the definition's 'especially God's commandments' qualifier is too restrictive.

'The commandment commanded (ἐντολῆς) by the Lord' represents the 'commanded' sense (sense 3), where the word is embedded in a verbal construction that the label 'an instruction given' inadequately captures.

audit.author_note: John (Gospel + 1–2 John, 28× combined) uses ἐντολή with a distinctly relational and love-focused framing ('this is my commandment, that you love one another'), whereas Paul (Romans, 1 Corinthians, Ephesians) tends to use it in a more forensic or salvation-historical argument about the law's function — readers moving between these authors may find the single definition insufficiently nuanced.

prose.def: Describing someone or something belonging to a particular place; a local person or resident.
prose.article: ἐντόπιος is built from ἐν ("in") and τόπος ("place"), so it simply means "of that place" — a local or resident. It appears only once in the New Testament, at Acts 21:12, where it blends into the phrasing rather than getting its own English word. The everyday Koine papyri make the sense vivid: people used it of "local purple" dye, gold weighed by the "local standard," and "native stone," while one document contrasts a list of locals (ἐντοπίων) with Alexandrians.
prose.caution: This word occurs only once in the New Testament, so its full range in biblical usage rests largely on outside papyri evidence.

prose.def: An adverb meaning 'within' or 'inside,' used of physical interiors and, disputedly, of the kingdom of God being within or among people.
senseLabels: the inside / interior (of a physical object)

prose.article: ἐντός is a small word built from ἐν ("in") that points to what is inside or within. In its two New Testament appearances it does double duty: in Matthew 23:26 it refers to the inside of a cup, while in Luke 17:21 it describes the kingdom of God being "within" or "among" you—a phrase that has been long disputed. Interestingly, Moulton-Milligan notes the very same phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν appears in an early non-biblical saying attributed to Jesus (P Oxy IV. 654), where the surrounding context favors the translation "within you."
prose.caution: With only 2 New Testament occurrences and a famously disputed sense in Luke 17:21 (translators split between "within you" and "among you"), this word's exact range is uncertain.

audit.author_note: Matthew uses ἐντός in a concrete spatial sense (inside of a vessel) while Luke uses it in a theologically charged adverbial phrase about the kingdom of God, suggesting meaningfully different registers across the two authors.

prose.def: To put someone to shame (active) or, in the middle/passive, to feel respect toward a person or to feel ashamed of one's own conduct.
prose.article: This verb carries two related shades: actively it means to put someone to shame, while in the middle or passive voice it means to feel respect or reverence toward a person. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 9 times across 7 books, and where the Majority Standard Bible gives it a clear English word, "respect" wins (LUK 18:4; 20:13). prose.caution: Only one English sense ("respect") could be cleanly measured from the renderings, and 2 of 9 occurrences were absorbed into phrasing, so the "put to shame" sense rests mainly on the lexica rather than the corpus counts.

prose.def: Shaking with fear, trembling because one is terrified.
prose.article: ἔντρομος describes someone physically shaking because they are afraid. It appears just 3 times in the New Testament (Acts 7:32, Acts 16:29, Heb 12:21), and across all three the Majority Standard Bible and the BSB consistently render it as some form of "trembling" or "trembling with fear." In the Septuagint it shows up twice and renders Hebrew words for shaking and quaking; interestingly, an ancient magical papyrus uses a closely related form (ἔκτρομος) to describe making the very foundations of the earth tremble.
prose.caution: Evidence is thin: only 3 New Testament occurrences and a low confidence tier, and the manuscripts vary at Heb 12:21 between ἔντρομος and ἔκτρομος.

prose.def: To revel or take delight in something, ranging from simple pleasure (papyri, LXX) to wanton, self-indulgent excess (2 Pet 2:13).

prose.def: To make a petition before an authority either in favor of someone (intercede) or against someone (lodge a complaint), depending on the accompanying preposition.

to appeal / lodge a complaint against someone (κατά)

prose.caution: With only three occurrences and a computed low confidence tier, the precise range of meaning rests on thin evidence.

prose.def: To be engraved or imprinted into a surface, leaving a permanent mark; used in the passive to describe letters cut into stone.

prose.def: To dream (used literally of receiving dreams in sleep, or pejoratively of those who indulge in self-deluding fantasies); deponent verb.
senseLabels: dreamers (pejorative participial use of those living in self-delusion)
prose.article: This verb means to dream or to experience visions while sleeping. In the New Testament it appears only twice—in Acts 2:17, where it describes old men dreaming dreams (quoting Joel), and in Jude 1:8, where it labels certain people as 'dreamers.' The word was at home in everyday Koine: Egyptian papyri even mention an ἐνυπνιοκριτής, a professional dream-interpreter at the Serapeum, showing how seriously dreams were taken. In the Septuagint it occurs 15 times and almost always translates the Hebrew חָלַם (to dream), 11 of those times.
prose.caution: With only two New Testament occurrences, the measured range is very thin, though the Septuagint and papyri evidence strongly agree on the basic meaning.

audit.author_note: Luke uses the word in a straightforward OT-citation context (Acts 2:17) referring to literal God-given dreams, while Jude uses it pejoratively of false teachers, suggesting a morally negative connotation absent in Luke's usage.

prose.def: A preposition meaning 'before,' 'in the presence of,' or 'in the sight of' a person or being, often God as witness or judge, sometimes absorbed into idiomatic phrasing.
prose.article: ἐνώπιον is a preposition built from "in" plus a word for "eye" or "face," so it literally puts you face-to-face with someone. The Byzantine NT uses it 96 times, and over half of those (53%) are simply rendered "before," while the rest cluster around closely related ideas of presence and sight — these are really shades of one core meaning rather than separate senses. It's a favorite of Luke, Acts, and Revelation but never appears in Matthew or Mark, and a common phrase is "in the sight of God," picturing God as the one watching or judging. The Septuagint uses it 454 times, most often to translate the Hebrew words for "face" (192×) and "eye" (114×), which fits its eye-and-face origins perfectly.

prose.def: Enosh, a biblical patriarch — the son of Seth and grandson of Adam.
prose.article: Ἐνώς is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Enosh, a personal name with only one meaning: it always refers to the patriarch who was Seth's son. It appears just once in the New Testament, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38), where the Majority Standard Bible renders it "Enosh" 100% of the time. In the Septuagint it shows up 7 times in 2 books, every instance translating the same Hebrew name אֱנוֹשׁ, first introduced in Genesis 4:26.
prose.caution: This is a proper name with a single fixed referent, so there is no real range of meaning to debate despite the low confidence tier.

receipts.how: The sole NT occurrence places Ἐνώς in Jesus's genealogy as the son of Seth, exactly matching the definition's identification of the patriarch.
